day-1.t: Day 1 — Decide what the report is for

b.v: Today's goal

v: Write the one question your report answers
Name the reader and how often they will open it
Agree what a good number looks like before you build anything

b.v: About 20 minutes. Paper and pen. Power BI Desktop can stay closed today.

A report nobody opens is a failure, however beautiful it is. Power BI makes it easy to build something impressive in an hour, so the temptation is to build first and ask later. Today you do the opposite, and it saves you a week.
1) One question, one reader

Write this sentence on paper: 'The shop owner opens this every Monday morning to decide which two products to reorder.' That sentence decides your data, your visuals and your refresh schedule. If you cannot write it, the report is not ready.
Do this now:|Write the reader's role and name|Write the day and time they will open it|Write the decision they will make|Write what they do today instead, such as asking you on WhatsApp
2) Agree the numbers before building

A report that shows 11,750 when the owner expects 9,500 gets closed and never reopened. Fix the definitions in writing first: which orders count, whether returns are subtracted, and which date is used.

v: Measure = a number in Power BI, such as total sales
Definition = the exact rule behind the measure, written in words
Period = the dates included, and whether it is the order date or the delivery date

v.cap: The data model you will build. Sales is the fact table, the other two are lookup tables.
rows: OrderID, OrderDate, CustomerID, ProductID, Quantity, UnitPrice, Status

b.v: Sales numbers used all course: 1001 has two lines (12 notebooks at 150 and 5 markers at 120), then 1200, 800, 2100, 3000 and 2250. The total is 11,750 rupees across five distinct orders.
3) Write the success test

Decide now how you will know the report worked. It is not 'it looks good'. It is something you can check in a month: the owner opened it four Mondays in a row, or reordered based on it, or stopped sending you the same question.
The most common beginner mistake is building for yourself. You like slicers and dark themes; the owner wants two numbers and a phone screen. Build for the reader, not for the demo.
Practice

Write a one-page brief: reader, question, decision, the three measures with their definitions, and the success test. Get one sentence of agreement from the person who will use it before Day 2. A WhatsApp message saying 'yes, that is what I need' is enough.

day-2.t: Day 2 — Import data and understand the three views

b.v: Today's goal

v: Import an Excel or CSV file into Power BI Desktop
Use the Report, Data and Model views without getting lost
Check row counts before trusting anything

b.v: About 20 minutes. Power BI Desktop is free to download and install on Windows.

Power BI Desktop is the free tool where you build reports. Three views sit on the left edge: Report for the page you show, Data for the tables, Model for the relationships. Everything you build lives in one .pbix file on your computer until you publish it.
1) Get the file in

Home, then Get data. For an Excel workbook choose Excel workbook; for a plain text file choose Text/CSV. Power BI shows a preview with the first rows, and you must click Load or Transform Data. Never click Load before you have looked at the preview.

Import and check:|Home, then Get data, then Excel workbook|Pick the file and tick the sheet|Look at the preview: are the headers correct and the dates red or black?|Click Transform Data if anything is wrong, or Load if it is clean|Note the row count in the Data view

v: Report view = where you place charts
Data view = the actual rows, good for spot checks
Model view = the diagram of how tables connect
Transform Data = opens Power Query, where cleaning happens

b.v: 2) Check the row count
In the Data view, Power BI shows how many rows each table has. If your Excel file has 7 sales lines and Power BI shows 8, you imported a total row or an empty row. Fix it now, not after three charts.

v.cap: Sales table as it should look after import, 7 rows

b.v: 3) Save the file properly
Press Ctrl+S and name the file with the business and the month, such as shop-sales-jan2026.pbix. Keep it in one folder you can find. A report called Book1.pbix on the desktop is nobody's friend.
If dates show as text, Power BI cannot group by month later. Go back to Power Query and set the column type to Date before loading. Fixing the type after loading is harder and often breaks measures.
Practice

Import your sales file and confirm it shows 7 rows and 6 columns with dates recognised as dates. Save as shop-sales-jan2026.pbix. Then click through all three views once and find where the row count is shown.

day-3.t: Day 3 — Clean the data in Power Query

b.v: Today's goal

v: Remove junk rows and fix data types in Power Query
Split one messy column into useful ones
Understand Applied Steps and why order matters

b.v: About 25 minutes. This lesson is the one that saves the most time later.

Power Query is the cleaning room next to the report. Every change you make there is recorded as a step, so next month you paste new data, press Refresh, and all the cleaning repeats by itself. No copy and paste, no forgotten formula.
1) Look at Applied Steps

On the right side, Applied Steps lists everything done to this table. Each step has a name, and you can click any step to see the table as it was at that moment. Click the gear icon to edit a step instead of deleting and redoing it.

First clean pass:|Right-click the first row and choose Use First row as headers if the header is below the top|Home, then Remove Rows, then Remove Blank Rows|Select each column and set the correct type with the icon at the left of the header|Rename any column that has a space or an odd capitalisation

v: Applied Steps = the recorded history of cleaning, run again on every refresh
Change Type = set text, whole number, decimal or date deliberately
Remove Errors = deletes rows that failed a type change, which you must review before deleting

b.v: 2) Split and trim

A column like Lahore - 54000 holds two facts. Split it by delimiter so you can group by city properly. Extra spaces at the start and end of text cause unmatched joins, and one Trim step removes them all.
3) A column of your own
Add a LineTotal column in Power Query as Quantity multiplied by UnitPrice. You can also add it later as a DAX calculated column, but doing it here keeps the model smaller and the file faster.
Do not sort a table in Power Query to 'make it look nice'. Sorting there is a step that runs on every refresh and does not affect the report's order anyway. Sort in the visual instead.
Practice

In Power Query, set types correctly, trim all text columns, add a LineTotal column, and confirm the table still has 7 rows. Then click the first Applied Step and the last, and watch the table change. Close and Apply, and check the row count again in the Data view.

day-4.t: Day 4 — Relationships: the shape of your model

b.v: Today's goal

v: Connect Sales to Customers and Products
Understand one-to-many and why direction matters
Add a separate Date table and mark it as a date table

b.v: About 25 minutes. Open the Model view and take your time.

A model is tables plus the links between them. Get the links right and every visual works. Get them wrong and you get totals that are quietly, confidently incorrect — the worst kind of wrong, because nobody notices for months.
1) Drag to connect

In Model view, drag CustomerID from Sales onto CustomerID in Customers. Power BI usually works out that Sales is the many side and Customers is the one side. The arrow shows the filter direction: Customers filters Sales, not the other way round.

v: One-to-many = one customer has many sales rows, the normal and healthy shape
Fact table = the table of events, here Sales, usually the biggest and the one with numbers
Lookup table = a small table of descriptions, here Customers and Products
Star schema = one fact table in the middle with lookup tables around it

b.v: 2) Keep it a star

Do not connect lookup tables to each other in a chain. A chain of relationships makes filters travel in strange ways and produces confusing totals. Put the fact table in the middle and point everything at it.

v.cap: The relationships you should see in Model view

b.v: 3) A real date table

Power BI can group by date on its own, but a separate date table gives you clean year, month and quarter columns that work in every visual. Create one with the modelling tools, connect it to Sales on the date column, then right-click it and choose Mark as date table.

Add the date table:|Modelling tab, then New table, and use the date table formula|Drag Date to OrderDate in Sales to create the link|Right-click the Date table and choose Mark as date table|Check that one Date row matches many Sales rows

Two relationships between the same two tables, or a relationship on the wrong column, will give you totals that look plausible and are wrong. Check with one number you already know: total sales must be 11,750.
Practice

Create both relationships and the date table. Then build a table visual with Customers Name and a quick sum of LineTotal. It must total 11,750. If it does not, look at the relationship arrows before changing any formula.
Today's goal

v: Write four measures: total sales, orders, average order, and target hit
Tell a measure from a calculated column
Use DIVIDE so a blank never crashes a report

b.v: About 25 minutes. Type the DAX by hand once — copying hides the learning.

DAX is the formula language of Power BI. A measure is a number calculated at the moment the visual needs it, using whatever filters are active. That is why one measure works for every city, month and product without being rewritten.
1) Measure or column?

A calculated column is computed once per row and stored in the table, so the file grows. A measure is computed on demand and stores nothing. If the answer depends on the filter on the page, it must be a measure.

v: Calculated column = per row, stored, good for LineTotal or a cleaned category
Measure = per visual, not stored, good for totals, averages and percentages
Context = the filters active when the measure runs

b.v: 2) The four measures
Right-click the Sales table, choose New measure, and type each one. The table name in square brackets tells Power BI where to look.

@DAX
Total Sales = SUM ( Sales[LineTotal] )

Orders = DISTINCTCOUNT ( Sales[OrderID] )

Average Order Value = DIVIDE ( [Total Sales], [Orders] )

Target Hit % = DIVIDE ( [Total Sales], 15000 )

v.cap: The four measures with no filter, checked by hand

b.v: Check the arithmetic yourself. 11750 divided by 5 is 2,350. 11750 divided by 15,000 is about 0.783, which displays as 78 percent. If your Orders measure shows 7, you counted lines instead of orders and you need DISTINCTCOUNT.
3) Why DIVIDE, not a slash
A plain slash returns an error when the bottom number is zero, and errors spread through a report. DIVIDE returns a blank instead, which simply leaves the cell empty and keeps the visual working.
Do not type numbers inside a measure unless it is a real target. 15000 above should ideally come from a Targets table so next month you change a row, not a formula.
Practice

Write all four measures and place them in four Card visuals. Confirm the values are 11,750, 5, 2,350 and 78 percent. Then add a fifth measure, Units Sold, as the sum of Quantity, and check it gives 65.

day-6.t: Day 6 — Visuals that answer the question

b.v: Today's goal

v: Pick the right visual for four common questions
Format a chart so it can be read in three seconds
Delete the defaults that add noise

b.v: About 20 minutes. Build slowly and delete more than you add.
Power BI will happily draw a pie chart with forty slices. It is your job to refuse. The visual is not decoration; it is the shape of an argument, and a bad shape makes a true number look false.
1) Match visual to question

v: How much in total = Card, one big number
Compare categories = bar chart, sorted, largest at the top
Change over time = line chart with a date on the axis
Two numbers against each other, such as sales and cost = a combo chart, used carefully

b.v: For our shop: total sales is a card, sales by city is a bar chart, sales by month is a line, and product performance is a small table. Four visuals answer four questions, and nothing else is needed.
2) Format for reading, not for showing off

Format one bar chart:|Click the visual, then the paintbrush icon|Turn off the title and write your own, such as Karachi leads with Rs 4,250|Set data labels on|Remove gridlines and the axis title if the labels are clear|Sort the visual by the value, not alphabetically

v.cap: City sales for the bar chart, sorted

b.v: These come from the customer table joined to sales: Ayesha in Lahore bought 2,400 and 2,100, so 4,500. Bilal in Karachi bought 2,000 and 2,250, so 4,250. Farhan in Multan bought 3,000. The three add to 11,750.
3) What to delete

v: Default titles that repeat the field name, such as Sum of LineTotal by City
Legends when there is only one series
Background shapes behind every visual
Axis titles when the labels already say it

b.v: Do not use a pie chart for more than five slices, and never use a 3D chart. Both make comparison harder, which is the opposite of what a report is for.
Practice

Build four visuals on one page: a card for total sales, a sorted bar chart by city, a line chart by month, and a table of product, units and sales. Give every visual a title that states a finding rather than a field name.
Today's goal

v: Add slicers that filter the whole page
Tell page filter, visual filter and slicer apart
Set up drill-through so one click shows the detail

b.v: About 20 minutes. Use the shop data you already loaded.
Filters turn one report into many answers. The risk is that a reader filters to one city, forgets, and believes sales collapsed. Good design makes the filter state obvious and the reset easy.
1) Three places filters live

v: Slicer = a visible control on the page, best for the reader
Page filter = hidden, applies to everything on that page
Visual filter = hidden, applies to one visual only
Report filter = applies to every page, good for the date range

b.v: Use a slicer when the reader will change it. Use a page or visual filter when the rule is fixed, such as hiding cancelled orders. Hidden filters are the reason a reader sometimes cannot match your total — so keep them few and write them in a note.
2) A slicer that behaves

Add and format a slicer:|Click empty canvas, choose the Slicer visual|Drop City into the field well|In the formatting pane, set the slicer to a horizontal list of buttons|Turn on Clear selection so one click resets|Add a text box beside it saying Filters: click a city to change all numbers

v.cap: What the page shows when the Lahore button is selected

b.v: Check the Lahore column: two orders, 2,400 and 2,100, so 4,500, and 4,500 divided by 2 is 2,250. Notice that the average changed too — that is the measure responding to the filter, which is the whole point of DAX.
3) Drill-through to the rows

Drill-through lets a reader right-click one product and jump to a second page that shows only that product's rows. Create a new page, put a table of orders on it, and drag ProductID into the Drill-through box. Rename the page Details.
If a slicer filters some visuals but not others, the visuals are on a different page or have a conflicting visual filter. Check the filter pane before rebuilding the slicer.
Practice

Add a City slicer and a Status slicer. Click Lahore and confirm total sales becomes 4,500 and average order 2,250. Then build a drill-through Details page and test it by right-clicking a product in your table visual.

day-8.t: Day 8 — Report layout that a phone can read

b.v: Today's goal

v: Lay out one page with a clear reading order
Design for a phone as well as a laptop
Write titles that state the finding

b.v: About 20 minutes. Use View, then Mobile layout at the end of the lesson.

Most readers in Pakistan will open your report on a phone. A page built only for a wide laptop screen arrives as a tiny mess of overlapping boxes. Designing for the small screen first makes the big screen better too.
1) The five-zone page

Keep one page, one idea. Put a title strip at the top, a row of key numbers under it, the main chart in the middle, a small table at the bottom, and the filter controls on the right or beside the title. Read your own page from top left and see if the story is in order.

Build the page:|Title strip: what this is and the date range|Three cards: sales, orders, target hit|One main chart: sales by city|One small table: product performance|Slicers grouped together, not scattered
2) The mobile layout

View, then Mobile layout gives you a tall phone-shaped canvas. Drag the visuals you want into it, in the order a thumb should scroll: title, numbers, chart, table. Anything you leave off is hidden on phones only.

v: Mobile layout = a separate arrangement for phones, not a smaller copy
Reading order = the sequence a reader follows, which should match the decision
White space = gaps that separate groups of information

v.cap: The layout as a simple map

b.v: 3) Titles that say something
Replace Sales by City with Lahore and Karachi bring 75 percent of sales. Now the reader gets the finding even if they only glance. A title is free space; use it for meaning, not for a field name.
Do not stack more than six visuals on one page. Beyond that, the reader stops reading and starts scrolling, and the report becomes a data dump with colours.
Practice

Finish your one-page report with the five zones, then arrange the mobile layout and look at it in phone view. Ask someone to open it on their phone and say the headline number out loud without scrolling.
Today's goal

v: Publish a report from Desktop to the Power BI service
Share with the right permission instead of sending files
Understand refresh and why a stale report is dangerous

b.v: About 20 minutes. You need a work or school account for publishing; the free Desktop app alone cannot share.

Publishing puts the report online so others can open it without installing anything. This is where a private file becomes a shared product, so permissions and refresh need a minute of thought, not a click and a hope.
1) Publish and check

In Desktop, click Publish and choose a workspace. Then open the report in the browser and look at it. Do not assume it looks the same: fonts, sizes and some formatting can shift, and better to find out before your manager does.

Publish and verify:|Home, then Publish, then pick the workspace|Open the link in a browser|Check every measure against the numbers you know, such as 11,750|Check the mobile view in the service too|Copy the link and keep it in one place
2) Share, do not attach

Sending a .pbix file on WhatsApp gives someone a frozen copy they can never refresh. Share the report link, or add people to the workspace, so everyone sees the same numbers. Use a security group rather than twenty individual names.

v: Workspace = the shared folder where reports live and permissions are set once
App = a packaged set of reports you publish to a group of readers
Direct link = a shareable address for one report, best for a small team

b.v: 3) Refresh or be wrong

A report is only as good as its last refresh. A file imported from Excel keeps the old numbers until it refreshes, and a report with yesterday's data can still look perfect. Set a scheduled refresh and check it actually ran.

v.cap: A short note you put on the report page, so nobody has to ask
rows: Shop Excel file, one row per order line
Daily, at the time set in the workspace
Returns are not yet in the model

b.v: Sharing a report that refreshes from your personal laptop means it stops updating the moment your laptop is off. Use a source that stays online, or accept that the numbers will be old and say so.
Practice

Publish your report, open it in the browser and verify 11,750 appears. Add the note above as a text box on the page. Then set a daily refresh and check the refresh history the next day to confirm it ran.

day-10.t: Day 10 — Why a report nobody opens is a failure

b.v: Today's goal

v: Measure whether your report is used, not whether it looks good
Run a short review with the reader and change one thing
Write a handover note so the report survives without you

b.v: About 20 minutes. Invite the reader for five minutes if you can.
You can build the most accurate report in the country and still fail, because nobody opens it. Success in reporting is a behaviour change, not a finished file. That is a hard lesson and a useful one.
1) Signs a report is being ignored

v: The reader still asks you the same question on WhatsApp
View counts are low or the last view was the day you sent it
They export to Excel and rebuild it themselves
They open it, look confused and close it without clicking a slicer

b.v: Each of these is information. The WhatsApp question usually means the report does not answer the question they actually have. The export habit usually means they do not trust a number or cannot filter the way they need.
2) The five-minute review

Sit with the reader:|Ask them to find the answer to one real question, without your help|Stay quiet and watch where they hesitate|Ask what they would change first|Change one thing only, and show it the next day|Repeat next month

v.cap: A simple adoption log. Honest numbers beat good intentions.
rows: Added target line to sales card

b.v: 3) Write the handover note

One page: where the data comes from, what each measure means, when it refreshes, what is missing, and who to call. Without it the report dies the week you change jobs, and so does your reputation for building useful things.
Do not keep adding pages to fix confusion. More pages usually makes it worse. Fix the one page the reader actually uses, and delete the rest.
Practice

Do the five-minute review with your reader. Write down the one thing they would change, make that change, and publish again. Then write your one-page handover note and store it beside the .pbix file. Finally, delete any visual on the page that nobody looked at.
